---
title: "What is agentic coding?"
---

## The shift in one paragraph

Until recently, using an LLM meant **typing into a chat box** and copy-pasting
the answer back into your editor. That works, but it puts you in the loop
for every small action: copy this, paste here, run it, paste the error back,
ask again. "Agentic coding" tools cut that loop. You give the model **direct
access to your project** — it can read files, edit them, run code, see the
output, and decide what to do next. You stay in the loop for *direction* and
*review*, not for clerical handoffs.

That is the whole shift.

## A concrete contrast

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Chat-style (what you might be doing now)**

> *You:* "Write me a Stata loop that runs a regression for each year and
> stores coefficients."
>
> *LLM:* (gives a snippet)
>
> *You:* (paste into Stata, hit run, get an error about a missing variable)
>
> *You:* "I got this error: `variable wage_resid not found`"
>
> *LLM:* (apologizes, gives a new snippet)
>
> *You:* (paste, run, repeat 3 more times)
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Agentic (what Claude Code does)**

> *You:* "Write a loop that runs my main regression for each year and stores
> the coefficients. Look at `analysis.do` to see how I've set up the
> covariates."
>
> *Claude Code:* (reads `analysis.do`, writes the loop, runs it, sees the
> `wage_resid not found` error, reads `02-build-vars.do`, notices that
> `wage_resid` is generated only when a flag is set, fixes the loop, runs
> it again, shows you the diff and the resulting coefficients)
:::

The chat version takes ten minutes of attention. The agentic version takes
ten minutes of clock time but maybe one minute of yours.

## What you give up, and what you keep

You give up the **moment-by-moment control** of every keystroke. You can't
inspect the model's reasoning step by step in real time, and you have to
trust that it's editing the right files in the right way.

You keep — and *must* exercise — **direction and review**. You decide what
to ask for. You read the diff — the exact lines that changed — before accepting it.
You run the regression
yourself before believing the number. See
[verifying output](../workflow/verifying.qmd).

## Why this matters for an economist specifically

It lands harder in our field than most:

1. **Our work is heavy on small, tedious code.** Renaming variables across
   a dozen `.do` files, regenerating tables in a different format, fixing
   a bibtex file with 200 entries — these are exactly the kinds of jobs
   where the agentic loop pays off.
2. **Reproducibility matters.** The model can read your whole replication
   package and tell you what's missing or what won't run on a fresh
   machine. A human RA would take a day; the model takes minutes.
3. **You probably have several projects in different languages.** The same
   tool works on Stata, R, Python, Matlab, Julia, LaTeX, and shell scripts
   — you don't need to learn a different assistant for each.

## What changes for your research workflow

What changes:

- Tedious code (variable renaming, table reformatting, replication-package
  cleanup, `.bib` fixes) takes minutes instead of hours.
- You stop avoiding small-but-annoying improvements ("I'll fix that figure
  formatting later") because the friction drops to near zero.
- A second pair of eyes is always available: "what's wrong with this
  regression specification?" gets a useful answer in seconds.
- Onboarding to an unfamiliar codebase — your old paper from five years
  ago, a coauthor's repo, a published replication package — gets much
  faster.

What does not change:

- Your responsibility for the **specification, identification, and
  interpretation**. The model can suggest; you decide.
- The need to **read the diff** before accepting code into your project.
- The need to **run the regression yourself** before believing the number
  in your table.
- Your **research taste** — what's interesting, what's worth doing. The
  model has none of it, and will happily help you do bad work efficiently.
